title: Measuring Prejudice: What Does the Instrument Capture?
summary: Two sequential experiments set in an invented country. In the first, the learner sees one simulated respondent's latency difference score, predicts how many candidates from one region that person shortlisted, and finds out - repeatedly, against a printed base rate, until the difference between a real average association and a useful individual prediction is something they have felt rather than been told. In the second, five instruments (self-report, latency, behavioural choice, informant report and institutional outcomes) are examined one at a time for what each directly observes, what is inferred from it, what alternatives remain and which claim it cannot support. Nothing on the page measures, scores or labels the person using it.
learningObjectives: State, for each of five instruments, what it directly observes before anybody interprets it.
Explain why a small average association supports no prediction about any individual.
Distinguish self-reported attitude, latency measures, observed behaviour and institutional outcomes as four different objects at four levels.
Identify why no individual attitude score can confirm or refute a claim about institutional discrimination.
Recognise the point at which an instrument stops being evidence about a construct and starts being treated as the construct.
interactionTypes: individual-case prediction against a base rate
scatter plot with full text and tabular equivalents
privacy: Every selection is held in the browser tab only and discarded when the page is left; nothing is saved, stored or transmitted. No task on the page measures, scores or labels the person using it - the sorting task is run only on fictional respondents, which is a design decision rather than an oversight.
accessibilityNotes: Nothing is timed and there is no reaction-time task for the learner to perform, so no part of the activity depends on motor speed. The scatter plot is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a sentence stating the correlation, the selected respondent's score and what a perfectly predictive score would look like, plus a full table of mean and range by outcome band and a printed rule-accuracy check. The selected respondent is marked by a ring and a full-height dashed stem, so it is found by shape and position rather than colour. Every control is a native radio or button in a labelled fieldset, and requesting a reveal without a prediction produces an explanatory message that treats 'you cannot tell from this score' as a real answer. Both experiments announce every change through the shell's polite live region, and either reset button restores the entire page including the prediction gate. Headings run h1 to h5 without skipping, focus moves to the first experiment's heading when the gate opens, targets are at least 2.75rem, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: A latency score, a shortlist, a survey and twelve years of appointment figures - four objects at four levels, and none of them is prejudice
simulationNotes: Vantry, the Uplands and the Lowlands are invented and stand for no real population anywhere; the setting was chosen to have no real-world referent so that nothing here can be read as a claim about any actual group. No figure on the page is a prevalence estimate, a norm or a published effect. Experiment 1 generates 200 respondents from mulberry32 seeded at 20260811 with Box-Muller normal draws: a latent association z is drawn, the latency difference score is 0.34 + 0.22z + 0.26e1 seconds, a behavioural latent is -0.30z + e2, the number of same-region candidates shortlisted is round(2 + 0.85 x behavioural latent) clamped to 0-4, and a self-reported warmth gap is 13 + 2.0z + 8e3 points. The construction gives a population correlation of about -0.19, deliberately of the same order as correlations reported in meta-analyses of real latency-behaviour relationships; rounding and clamping attenuate the realised sample value to -0.12. The sample median score is 0.32 s; 43 per cent of the 200 shortlists were even, and a rule that reads a score above the median as 'fewer' is right for 57 per cent of the 114 respondents whose shortlist was not even. The automated twenty-trial run, which always follows the score's direction, typically lands near 25 per cent against that 43 per cent base rate. Every reported figure is computed from the generated sample at run time rather than written into the page. The five instrument findings in experiment 2 are authored for teaching and no published study, dataset or instrument is reproduced or referred to.
